new_statements.quote: Doch daartusschen en, wat op hetzelfde nederkomt, tusschen de syllaben van een tweelettergrepig woord bestaat, wat den klemtoon aangaat, geen essentieel verschil. Dat wil zeggen: het accent heeft er geen vaste plaats; want bijkomende omstandigheden bewerken dat het nu eens op de voorlaatste dan weder op de laatste lettergreep wordt waargenomen. Op de keper beschouwd kent het Madoereesch, behoudens hetgeen omtrent de derde lettergreep van achteren is medegedeeld, derhalve geen eigenlijken syllaben-klemtoon; de nadruk op een lettergreep in een bepaald geval is niets anders dan een uitvloeisel van de gemoedsgesteldheid of bijzondere inzichten van den spreker (oratorisch accent).
new_statements.translation: But between these [the last two syllables of a prefixed trisyllable] and, what comes to the same thing, between the syllables of a disyllabic word there is, as far as stress is concerned, no essential difference. That is to say: the accent has no fixed place there; for incidental circumstances cause it to be perceived now on the penultimate, now on the final syllable. Strictly speaking, then, Madurese - apart from what has been said about the third syllable from the end - has no real syllable stress; the emphasis on a syllable in a given case is nothing but an outflow of the mood or particular intentions of the speaker (oratorical accent).
new_statements.citation: Kiliaan, H. N. 1897. Madoereesche spraakkunst. Eerste stuk: Inleiding en klankleer. Batavia: Landsdrukkerij. § 111 'Klemtoon', pp. 83-84.
new_statements.locator: Eerste stuk, § 111 (Klemtoon), pp. 83-84 (scanned the text; secondary accent § 115, p. 85; exceptions §§ 112-114, pp. 84-85)
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: present at the stated locator, lines 4939-4951 (§ 111 'Klemtoon', printed pp. 83-84; scan = archive.org madoereeschespr01kiligoog, Google scan of Kiliaan 1897 Madoereesche spraakkunst vol. 1, OCLC 26625440). Only scanned-level differences: 'kent bet Madoereesch' for 'kent het Madoereesch', spacing 'Dat wil zeggen :'; wording otherwise identical. The translation and rule_in_words are accurate; §§ 112-115 (lines 4953-5051: penult tendency in trisyllables, antepenult never accented without a glide, penult in exclamations, final in vocatives/calls, main + secondary accent in 4+-syllable words) and the § 113 Aanmerking rejecting the 'penult unless schwa' rule (lines 5015-5036) are as repo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Madurese as a whole Kiliaan denies a fixed word stress: in disyllables and in the last two syllables of trisyllables the accent falls on the penult or the final according to the speaker's emphasis; the only firm restriction is that the antepenult (third from the end) is never accented (unless a j/w glide can be inserted before suffix -an); trisyllabic roots and prefixed words tend toward the penult but may take final accent. He explicitly rejects the 'penult unless it has schwa' rule as an observer's illusion (§ 113 Aanm., p. 85).
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 115 (p. 85): words of four or more syllables are pronounced in at least two parts, each with its own accent, so a secondary accent (bijaccent) can be distinguished from the main accent, e.g. ndroq-aghijq with main on ghi- and secondary on no-, or the reverse; there is a noticeable tendency to accent the last syllable of the first part.
new_statements.exceptions: § 112: trisyllables by suffix tend to penult but final also occurs (mentaqa ~ mentaqa'); antepenult never accented without a glide. § 113: in exclamations of astonishment the penult takes the accent and is lengthened. § 114: in calls and exclamations (vocatives, hawkers' cries, swear-words) the accent falls on the final syllable. Monosyllabic prefixes are proclitic and unaccented (§ 111).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, but the statement is about MADURESE as spoken on the main island (West and East Madurese); Kiliaan classes Kangean as a sub-dialect of East Madurese (Inleiding V, p. 11) and states on p. 12 that Kangean-specific phenomena are 'afgehandeld' and the following chapters (including § 111) concern the language of the main island. No Kangean-specific stress statement was found in any opened source.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Kiliaan 1897 § 111) describes Madurese of the main island (nucl1460: West Madurese = Pamekasan/Bangkalan, East Madurese = Sumenep). Kiliaan treats Kangean (kang1289) as a sub-dialect of East Madurese and explicitly sets Kangean-specific phenomena aside before the chapter containing § 111 (Inleiding, p. 12). No opened source states where word stress falls in Kangean itself; the only Kangean description (Soegianto et al. 1986) could not be accessed.

sources.note: Inleiding V e (pp. 11-12) lists seven features of the Kangean sub-dialect (vowel quality, nasal prefix a-, passive di-, suffix -aghen/-aken, possessive -na, reduplication, lexical correspondences) and says nothing about stress; p. 12 states the following chapters treat the main-island language. §111 (pp. 83-84): in Madurese the accent has no fixed place (penult or final depending on circumstances); apart from the antepenult never being accented, Madurese has no real syllable stress, only oratorical accent; trisyllables tend to penult (§112); exclamations penult (§113), vocatives final (§114);…

sources.citation: Sofyan, Akhmad. 2010. Fonologi Bahasa Madura. Humaniora 22(2): 207-218. (Wikipedia mis-cites this as 'Fonologi Bahasa Kangean'.)
sources.note: Segmental phonology of Madurese (vowels, consonants, diphthongs, clusters, phonotactics); no section on stress/tekanan. p. 216 fn. 6 summarises Soegianto et al. 1986 on the Kangean dialect: very fast pronunciation, phonological rules unlike the other dialects, many lexical differences, suffix -na does not assimilate; nothing on stress. Reference list (pp. 217-218) gives Soegianto et al. 1986 as an unpublished research report and Sariono et al. 1997 Unsur Prosodi dalam Bahasa Madura.
